evals.prompt: This order sync module is a mess and I think it has a real bug in it somewhere. Can you sort it out? (attached: orders.ts)
evals.expected_output: Runs the detectors first rather than reading by hand, and triages the mechanical findings before judgment. Separates real defects from debt and leads with the defects: `ids.forEach(async id => await this.syncOne(id))` never waits and loses every rejection; the catch block logs to console and returns null, so a failed sync is indistinguishable from an empty one; `decorate` mutates the caller's record in place and multiplies `total` behind a non-null assertion; `config.lastRun = …` mutates an imported module; `export let lastSyncedAt` is a live mutable binding importers see change under them. Also flags the hardcoded `sk-live-…` API key default as a credential in source. Only then raises the debt: `as any` on the parsed response with no validation at the boundary, the all-optional `OrderRecord` that permits `{}` and should be a discriminated union on `status`, the `status ===` if/else ladder that the union would make exhaustive, `public cache` plus `getCache()` handing out the live Map, the `(id, name, region)` data clump repeated across three functions, and the index loop that is a `map`. Says which findings it verified by hand. Does not claim the code is fixed without running `tsc --noEmit` and the tests.

evals.prompt: Our tsconfig has strict: false and there are about 4000 errors when I turn it on. Everyone says we should just leave it off. What do you think?
evals.expected_output: Loads references/strictness-migration.md rather than answering from general opinion. Does not accept 'leave it off' and does not propose a big-bang branch either. Explains what specifically is lost — with strictNullChecks off every type silently includes null and undefined, so the compiler cannot warn about the most common runtime error class — and separates the nine flags by value, putting strictNullChecks and noImplicitAny far above the rest. Proposes the ratchet: a second tsconfig with an allowlist (or the strict plugin) so new code is strict immediately, noImplicitAny before strictNullChecks because it is mechanical, leaf modules before hubs, and a CI check on the error count that only goes down. Warns explicitly that a migration landing with hundreds of new `!` and `@ts-expect-error` has moved the problem rather than fixed it. Acknowledges the cost honestly rather than presenting it as free.

evals.prompt: Can you replace every `for (const x of xs) { await f(x) }` in the codebase with Promise.all? Should be a nice speedup.
evals.expected_output: Agrees the loops are worth finding (find_async_issues.py, await_in_loop) but refuses a blanket mechanical replacement. Loads references/async-and-concurrency.md and names what the change breaks: iterations where each step depends on the previous one's output, endpoints that rate-limit, side effects whose ordering matters, and unbounded fan-out over a large list opening thousands of connections at once. Points out that Promise.all abandons the remaining work on the first rejection, which is a behaviour change even when the loop was genuinely independent. Goes through the loops and says which are safe, rather than converting all of them, and suggests a bounded concurrency pool where the list is large. Treats a one-line comment explaining a deliberate sequential loop as the right outcome for the ones that must stay.

evals.prompt: Review my code. [pastes a TypeScript service class with an IUserService interface implemented once, a UserServiceImpl with a single public method and no fields, and a UserServiceFactory that returns new UserServiceImpl()]
evals.expected_output: Recognises the whole stack as ceremony around one function and says so directly. Uses the structural-typing argument specifically: an interface is not needed to mock in TypeScript because any object of the right shape satisfies the parameter, so 'I need it for tests' is not a reason to keep it. Recommends deleting the interface, the factory and the class, leaving an exported function. Flags the `I` prefix as against TypeScript convention. Does not hedge with 'it depends on your team's preferences' — but does name the genuine exceptions (a published package boundary, a plugin contract, two real implementations) so the user can check whether any applies. Loads references/overengineering-and-abstraction.md rather than reasoning from Java habits.

evals.prompt: Here's a PR from an AI agent adding a caching layer. It compiles and the tests pass. Can you review it?
evals.expected_output: Treats compiling and green tests as the starting condition rather than as evidence, and says so. Runs analyze_diff.py for findings on the changed lines and find_ai_scaffolding.py, and runs `tsc --noEmit` over the whole project rather than trusting that the change type-checks in isolation. Looks specifically for the generated-code tells: casts on parsed data with no validation beside them, an options parameter the body never reads, a `throw new Error('Not implemented')` that satisfies an interface, a duplicate definition where the later one silently wins, try/catch that logs and continues, and plausible constants (a TTL, a max size) with no stated origin. Reads the tests hard and checks that they can fail — breaking the implementation on purpose — rather than counting them. Checks each claim in the PR description against the diff. Does not reject the code for being generated; applies the same bar as any other change, to the parts the compiler could not check.

evals.prompt: We have index.ts barrel files in every folder and someone says they're causing our slow test startup. Are they worth keeping?
evals.expected_output: Loads references/modules-and-dependencies.md. Confirms the mechanism concretely rather than agreeing vaguely: importing one symbol from a barrel loads every module in the folder synchronously along with their imports, which is exactly why a test file ends up needing a mock for something it never uses. Adds the costs the user did not mention — barrels are the most common way an import cycle appears by accident (a file inside the folder importing from its own index), `export *` hides which module owns a name and collides silently, and tree shaking degrades. Distinguishes the one defensible case: a single explicit entry point for a published package, with named re-exports rather than `export *`. Recommends importing from the defining module inside the application, and suggests verifying with find_module_issues.py or madge --circular rather than asserting the cycles exist.

evals.prompt: Run your TypeScript analysis over this repo please. [a repo with no tests]
evals.expected_output: Runs find_tsconfig_issues.py first, because strictness changes how every other finding should be read. Runs analyze_all.py and also run_external_tools.py, and is explicit that the detectors read syntax rather than types, so tsc and typescript-eslint's type-aware rules cover what they structurally cannot. Treats `no_tests_at_all` as a blocker rather than one finding among many: says that refactoring without a safety net is rewriting and hoping, and that characterization tests for the highest-churn modules come before any of the cleanup. Orders the remaining work by churn × severity using git log rather than by finding count, and puts correctness bugs above style. Produces an artifact (list, cards or JSON) rather than editing files unasked, and asks which tracker to use before creating any tickets. Names any tool that was missing instead of implying it ran, and asks before installing anything.
